title: Upper Lower Light/Heavy 4 days split with mirror Week program review (part. 2)
summary: NH reviews the heavy/light second week of viewer Joelle's mirrored upper/lower program. He likes the volume adjustments around heavy and light openers but argues heavy/light days push intensity to extremes, recommends evolving rep ranges and A/B weeks with exercise variations instead, and discusses frequency versus session volume.
claims: When the opening lift is light, back-off work must make up the lost tonnage, and when it is heavy, back-off sets should be lighter: this is tonnage stability
Going from 4x4-6 to 4x8-10 on weighted pull-ups roughly doubles tonnage at the low end
Overhead pressing has almost no impact on weighted pull-up strength, so the pull-ups can still be taken near failure
The weight used for 6 reps must be heavier than for 10; using the same load means one set reaches failure and the other does not
3 sets of 8-10 is easier to progress on than 4 sets because intensity and endurance must be reproduced fewer times
Whenever you use static rep ranges you could replace them; if you want static tonnage, do heavy work in an evolving rep range then add back-off sets like 5x5 or 3x3
His overarching issue with the program is sandbagging, often without even freeing room for tonnage elsewhere
If the squat gets heavier, consider cutting one set of RDLs on that day
Heavy/light and volume/intensity days tend to be too extreme: too many irrelevant reps on volume days and too many grinding sets on heavy days, sabotaging progression
If heavy/light training stalls, drop it and use evolving rep ranges, which manipulate volume and intensity less arbitrarily; even one heavy set beats four sandbagged ones
Programs should keep flexibility; remove parameters that are not needed to open room for freedom
Instead of a heavy and light week, make week B use exercise variations, rotated rep ranges or muscle rotations, as in his Chico-inspired program; an 8-day cycle feels fresh
The deadlift needs the least frequency and regresses technically the least; skipping conventional pulls for 10 days does not hurt, unlike the bench
A light trap bar deadlift day is questionable since the trap bar is already a non-invasive variation you can go heavy on
Minimalism in programming is a tool to free time to train more muscles, not just to finish in 40 minutes
Training six days a week is already high and excellent
Shrinking to four or five days and packing more volume into each session builds endurance, so tonnage is higher when you later add days back; there are only seven days in a week to expand into
Adding a sixth day by spreading existing tonnage is an easier adaptation for the body than jamming more volume into seven days
Overall this is a solid program worth running
exercises: non-invasive, safer deadlift variation; can be heavy
drop reps from 10-12 to 6-8 on heavy day
